summary.text: Temperate climates are found in the middle latitudes, roughly 23.5° to 66.5° north or south of the Equator, between the tropics and the polar regions.
Compared with tropical climates, they usually have wider temperature ranges through the year and more distinct seasons.
Besides latitude, sea currents, prevailing winds, the size of the landmass and altitude all shape what a temperate place is like.

items.prompt: Hills in coastal California turn brown every summer and green again in winter. What rainfall pattern explains this?

options.label: Dry all year with rare storms

items.explain: Coastal California has a Mediterranean climate, which has a dry summer and a wet winter.

items.prompt: Two temperate cities share a latitude: one on a coast fed by cool ocean air, one deep inside a huge continent. Which gets the hotter summers and colder winters?

options.label: The coastal city, from damp sea air
The inland city, far from the sea
Whichever one sits at lower altitude

items.explain: Onshore flow from cool oceans gives mild summers and cool winters, while large land masses create a hot summer and a cold winter.

items.prompt: In some monsoon areas of southern China, how much of the year's precipitation falls in the five warmest months?
items.explain: These subtropical monsoon areas have a sharp wet-dry pattern, with very heavy summer rain and chilly, dry winters.

items.prompt: What brings the dry summers to places with a Mediterranean climate?

options.label: Dry winds from deserts on the side nearer the equator
Cold polar air that is too chilly to hold moisture
High mountains that block every wind off the sea
Sea water that grows too warm to make any clouds

items.explain: Mediterranean regions border arid deserts on their equatorward side, and those deserts bring the dry winds behind the summer dry season.

items.prompt: An oceanic-climate town sits much closer to the pole than most others of its type. What should it expect compared with them?
items.explain: Subpolar oceanic areas sit on the cool end of oceanic climates, and snowfall is more common there than in other oceanic climates.

items.prompt: A city lies at 30° N, in the warm band of the temperate zone nearest the tropics. What kind of weather is unusual there?
items.explain: Between 23.5° and 35° the temperate zone is strongly influenced by the tropics, and freezing precipitation is uncommon there.

beats.title: Same latitude, different seasons
beats.hook: Two cities can sit at the same distance from the equator, yet one has mild, damp winters while the other freezes and then bakes.

beats.prompt: A temperate town sits where air flows onshore from a cool ocean to its west. What are its seasons like?
beats.explain: Onshore flow from cool high-latitude oceans gives oceanic climates mild summers, cool winters, and humidity and rain spread through the year.

choices.label: A long dry winter and a very wet summer
choices.feedback: That is a monsoon pattern, not the effect of cool ocean air.

choices.label: Hot summers and bitterly cold winters
choices.feedback: That pattern comes from large land masses, not from steady onshore ocean air.

choices.label: Mild summers, cool but not cold winters, rain all year
A dry summer and a wet winter
choices.feedback: That is the Mediterranean pattern, set by nearby deserts in summer.

beats.explain: The temperate zone spans between the tropics and the polar regions; its subtropical band lies between 23.5° and 35°, and its cooler band between 35° and 66.5°.

beats.prompt: Sort each climate into its part of the temperate zone.
beats.explain: Some classifications split the temperate zone into a subtropical zone of humid subtropical and Mediterranean climates and a cool temperate zone of oceanic and continental climates.

paragraphs.heading: The middle band of the Earth
paragraphs.text: Temperate climates belong to Earth's middle latitudes, roughly 23.5° to 66.5° north or south of the Equator, between the tropics and the polar regions. In the north the zone runs from the Tropic of Cancer up to the Arctic Circle. In the south it runs from the Tropic of Capricorn down to the Antarctic Circle.

paragraphs.heading: Wider swings, many controls
paragraphs.text: Compared with the tropics, temperate places usually swing through a wider range of temperatures in a year and have clearer seasons. Tropical seasons often differ mainly in how much rain falls. Latitude is not the only control. Sea currents, the direction of the prevailing wind, continentality (how big the landmass is) and altitude all shape a temperate climate too.

paragraphs.heading: Drawing the line with Köppen
paragraphs.text: In the Köppen climate classification, a climate counts as temperate, letter C, when its coldest month averages above −3 °C but below 18 °C, a limit meant to reflect lasting frost. Some versions of the scheme set the lower limit at 0 °C instead. A broader definition can also take in continental climates, letter D, which are more extreme, with the coldest month usually below −3 °C.

paragraphs.heading: The warm side
paragraphs.text: Some schemes split the zone into smaller ones based on monthly temperatures, the coldest month and rainfall. The subtropical part, between about 23.5° and 35°, feels the tropics most: summers are longer and hotter, winters shorter and milder, and freezing precipitation is uncommon. It holds two climates. Humid subtropical places have long, hot, humid summers with frequent showers and the most rain in the hottest months. Mediterranean places do the reverse, with dry summers and wet winters.

paragraphs.heading: The cool side
paragraphs.text: The cool temperate part lies between about 35° and 66.5° and also has two types, a milder oceanic one and a harsher continental one. Oceanic climates come from cool ocean air flowing ashore from the west. That gives mild summers, cool but not cold winters, and rain spread through the year, often under cloudy skies. Continental climates are made by large landmasses and winds that change direction with the seasons, so they swing between a hot summer and a cold winter.

paragraphs.heading: Where to find each one
paragraphs.text: Real places show the pattern. Coastal California, central Chile and the Western Cape of South Africa have Mediterranean climates. Northwestern Europe and most of New Zealand are oceanic. Southeastern Canada, Japan and the Korean Peninsula are humid continental.
